concepts.note: CORS is not authentication: it loosens the browser's same-origin rule for the origins named — anyone can still call the API from a non-browser client. The origin in the template is a TODO only you can choose: a wildcard (*) together with cookies or tokens is the footgun; named origins are the safe shape.

The token's claims are trusted only AFTER the signature and the expiry check out — before that they are text a stranger typed. Production systems usually take a maintained JWT library (an external dependency you add yourself); this hand-rolled HS256 check is the honest small-server shape, and it reads the secret from the environment, never from code.

The nonce is minted fresh from crypto/rand for every request and dies with it: a script copied from yesterday's page — or injected by an attacker — carries the wrong value and the browser refuses it. The policy also pins everything else to your own origin ('self').

Go 1.25's net/http has this built in — http.NewCrossOriginProtection checks where a request came from instead of comparing tokens — but it only compiles into projects whose go.mod says go 1.25 or newer. This row is the double-submit token shape every project can take; on go 1.25+, prefer the built-in.

Headers only speak to browsers, and only when set before the answer is written — wrap the OUTERMOST handler with this so every route gets them. HSTS stays a TODO in the template on purpose: it is HTTPS-only, and a browser that hears it remembers — sending it while you still test over plain http locks you out of your own site.

Visitors are counted by the address the request arrives from: behind a proxy or a shared office NAT, many people share one address and so share one count. A fixed window also means a burst straddling the boundary can briefly double the limit. A busy production API usually reaches for golang.org/x/time/rate (an external package); this is the honest small-server shape.

Anyone can READ a JWT's claims — the signature proves they weren't changed, it does not hide them — so a token never carries a password or a secret. And the signing secret here comes from the JWT_SECRET environment variable: a secret written in code is a secret published with the code.

Run this check on EVERY way in — read, change, delete, download — not just the page that shows the record: an attacker aims at whichever door was left unchecked. Making ids unguessable (random instead of counting up) slows the guessing down, but this check is the actual lock.

The session handler sets this same cookie with none of the flags set. These flags are the difference between a cookie that other sites and stray scripts can abuse and one they can't — and Secure is the one that bites in testing: over plain http on a non-localhost address the browser silently refuses the cookie, which looks exactly like the cookie code not working.

This builds the server value but starts nothing: the fields are the whole piece. The timeouts are also a promise about your own handlers — a handler slower than WriteTimeout is cut off mid-answer, so the numbers belong above your slowest honest page, not below it.

A request that crosses the limit fails its READS — the handler hears it as an error from reading or ParseForm, and hears nothing at all if it never reads the body. The limit only guards a handler that actually consumes what was sent.

source: Gollemer's concept book — names of code mapped to their basic code. Rows are data, not grammar: add a row (id, names, kind, template) and the composer can assemble that concept in every phrasing its slots allow, with no new Go code. A malformed row is skipped; the rest of the book still loads.
